opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing that matters is being honest about the problem you're actually trying to solve. In robotics it's very easy to fall in love with a method, like a new learning algorithm or a new model architecture, and then go looking for a problem to apply it to. The systems that work well usually start from the task and the environment. What does the robot need to do, what will it encounter, and what does success really look like?

The second thing is that a robot is a system, not a single model. You have perception, state estimation, planning, control, and the hardware itself, and they all interact. A small error in perception can turn into a big failure in control. So you need to think about the whole pipeline: where uncertainty enters, how errors propagate, and where you need robustness versus where you can get away with something simple. A lot of my work on imitation learning and long-horizon manipulation came from seeing that structure matters. If you decompose a task the right way, the learning problem becomes much more tractable.

Third, and this has become more and more important, is data. How you collect it, how diverse it is, and whether it actually covers the situations the robot will face. We've learned from language and vision that scale helps a lot, but in robotics data is expensive and physical. So designing good data collection systems, good teleoperation interfaces, and ways to reuse data across tasks and robots is a core part of building a good system, not an afterthought.

Finally, I'd say you have to test in the real world early and often. Simulation is incredibly useful, but reality always finds the assumptions you didn't know you were making. The groups that build great robots iterate quickly between ideas and real deployment, and they treat failures as the most informative signal they have.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics components interact and that errors can propagate, but it does not state that neglecting any single part will cause problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that what matters most is getting the whole stack to work together, not just one impressive piece of it.

A lot of people, especially coming from machine learning, want to treat robotics as a modeling problem. Train a bigger policy, collect more data, and the robot will figure it out. And data does matter enormously. But a robot lives in a closed loop with the physical world. Perception errors compound into control errors, latency shows up in ways your offline benchmark never showed, and the distribution you trained on quietly drifts the moment the lighting changes or someone moves a chair. So the first thing that matters is thinking about the system end to end, from how data gets collected, to how the policy makes decisions, to how it recovers when it's wrong.

The second thing is choosing the right level of abstraction. In my own work I've spent a lot of time on long-horizon manipulation, and one lesson that keeps coming back is that you don't want a single monolithic model to do everything. You want some structure. Maybe a higher-level reasoning component that decomposes a task into steps, and lower-level skills that are learned and robust. The question is always where to put the learning and where to put the structure, and the answer changes as models get better. Five years ago you needed a lot of hand-designed structure. Now foundation models can absorb a lot of that. But I don't think it ever goes to zero.

The third thing, and maybe the most underrated, is data and evaluation. How you collect demonstrations, who collects them, how diverse they are, and whether your evaluation actually reflects deployment. It's very easy to build something that works beautifully in the lab on the ten objects you tested and then falls apart on the eleventh. A good robotics system is one where you've been honest with yourself about generalization from the start.

And finally, I'd say humility about failure. Robots will fail. The question is whether the failure is graceful, detectable, and recoverable. Systems that are designed assuming perfection tend to be the most brittle ones.

r001.rationale: The response says the whole robotics stack must work together, not just one impressive component, and explains how perception errors can become control errors. This communicates that neglecting a part can cause system problems.

astra-6.text:
I think what matters most is how the pieces work together. In robotics, you have perception, planning, control, and the hardware itself. You can have a very strong algorithm for one part, but if its assumptions don’t match what the other parts can actually deliver, the whole system can fail.

So I would start with the task: What does the robot need to do, and under what conditions? Then build the simplest complete system you can test in the real world. Those tests help you understand where the bottleneck really is. Maybe you need better perception, but maybe you need a different gripper or a way to recover when a grasp fails.

A good system isn’t just one that succeeds in a carefully arranged demonstration. It should handle variation, recognize when something has gone wrong, and recover. That takes a lot of attention to the interfaces between components and to the details you only discover by running the robot.

r001.rationale: The candidate says mismatched assumptions between components can make the whole system fail, but does not state that neglecting any single part will cause problems.

sol-6.1.text: I think what matters is how all the pieces work together. You can have a great perception model or a great controller, but the robot has to close the loop: observe what happened, act, and adjust when something doesn’t go as expected. So I would start with the task and the environment, then design the hardware, the learning system, and the evaluation around that. And I’d pay a lot of attention to failures. A compelling demo is useful, but understanding when the system fails—and whether it can recover—is what helps you build something reliable.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot depends on its pieces working together, but it does not clearly state that neglecting any single part will cause problems.
